parts.article:
The origin of language
 
The archaeologist Stephen Mithen talks about the ideas behind his new book on the origin of language.
 
(A) Theories on the origin and evolution of language have been a major area of my research for many years. By 1859, when British scientist Charles Darwin published The Origin of Species, there was already a great deal of interest in this subject. However, the debate became plagued by strange theories, so much so that in 1866 the influential Société de Linguistique de Paris banned all discussions about the origin of language. The ban lasted for more than a century, before a surge of research began during the 1990s. Linguists, psychologists, anthropologists and archaeologists now frequently debate the origin of language and have published many articles and books on this topic. And yet, despite almost frenzied activity, limited progress has been made.
 
(B) I believe there are four reasons for this. The first is an insufficient concern with the archaeological and fossil proof of the brains and behaviour of our human ancestors. Many theories to date rely on an assumed association between brain size and language abilities, without acknowledging the problem this creates: fossil evidence indicates that the Neanderthals had larger brains than modern humans, Homo sapiens, but archaeological evidence indicates that the Neanderthals lacked a capacity for language. So something is seriously amiss with those theories.
 
(C) That 'something' might relate to the second reason for limited progress: insufficient concern with the other major aural and vocal communication system of modern humans: music. Even though the Société de Linguistique de Paris had nothing to say about studying the origin of music, academics appear to have had a self-imposed ban, with limited discussion of this issue during the 19th and 20th centuries. However, there are notable exceptions that should be acknowledged. One is the aforementioned Charles Darwin who, in his 1871 book on human evolution, The Descent of Man, devoted several pages to the development of music. Another is the renowned ethnomusicologist John Blacking, whose 1973 book, How Musical is Man?, broached the idea that music is an inherent and universal human quality.
 
(D) The origin of music deserves as much attention as that of language, as we cannot treat one without the other. Those writers who had evidently annoyed the Société de Linguistique de Paris were quite aware of this. For them, music and language were intimately linked; the French writer and philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau's On the Origin of Language (1781) was a reflection on both music and language. In contrast, Morten Christiansen and Simon Kirby's book, Language Evolution (2000), which they conceived as 'a definitive book on the subject', failed to mention music in any of its 17 chapters. Those authors have an important lesson to learn from Rousseau and other writers of his time who addressed the origin of language.
 
(E) Music is a universal feature of human society and plays a significant role in the lives of all individuals. Indeed, music is perhaps in even greater need of study than language: the latter has a self-evident function—the transmission of information—and can be readily accepted as a product of evolution, even if its specific evolutionary history remains unclear. But what is the point of music?
 
(F) That question leads directly to a third reason for our lack of progress in understanding how language evolved, and indeed the human mind in general: an insufficient concern with emotion. If music is about anything, it is about expressing emotion. But while archaeologists have put significant effort into examining the intellectual capacities of our ancestors, their emotional lives have been sorely neglected. This has contributed to the neglect of music, which, in turn, has constrained our understanding of language.
 
(G) There is one further reason why progress has been limited: those who have been most influential regarding the evolution of language have simply got it wrong, and misled everyone else. Linguist Derek Bickerton has made an important contribution towards our understanding of the origin of language by bringing his profound knowledge of linguistics to the discussions that have occurred. But Bickerton's idea that the precursor of modern language consisted of words strung together with limited, if any, grammar is, I believe, fundamentally mistaken. Bickerton refers to this precursor as 'proto-language' and suggests that it was similar to the type of language spoken by young children today, and mastered by apes through the use of computer keyboards. This idea has dominated the field of language origins for the last two decades, and is one that I once found persuasive. But I now understand that it is not only flawed but has severely limited the progress that should have been made.
 
(H) My book therefore provides an alternative view, one that draws on the ideas of a linguist who has, I believe, identified the true nature of proto-language. Her name is Alison Wray. She argues that proto-language was 'holistic' rather than compositional in character. By this she means that the precursor to language was a communication system composed of 'messages' rather than words; each message was uniquely associated with an arbitrary meaning, as are the utterances of language today. But in Wray's proto-language, they were not composed out of smaller units of meaning (i.e. words) which could be combined together using a rule system (i.e. grammar) to make more complex messages with emergent meanings. For Wray, proto-language was semantically complex and agrammatical. I believe this insight enables us to understand the origin of music as well as language, and to relate both to the emotional lives of our human ancestors.
parts.questions:
Questions 27–31
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

Q27 In the first paragraph, what does the writer suggest about the origin of language?

  • A Too many branches of science have been involved in its study.
  • B The Société de Linguistique de Paris instigated research in this area.
  • C The lack of progress is surprising given the amount of work being done.
  • D Most progress in the study of language was made between 1859 and 1866.

Q28 What is the ‘problem’ referred to in the second paragraph?

  • A Some current theories are based on conflicting evidence.
  • B There is insufficient fossil evidence to reach a conclusion.
  • C Fossil evidence suggests that Homo sapiens had larger brains than Neanderthals.
  • D Archaeological evidence shows that Neanderthals were able to talk.

Q29 What does the writer suggest about Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s work in 1781?

  • A Modern theorists should pay more attention to his approach.
  • B His ideas supported those of the Société de Linguistique de Paris.
  • C His ideas were mirrored in a later book called Language Evolution.
  • D His ideas are too outdated to be of any relevance today.

Q30 What is the writer’s current view of Derek Bickerton’s ideas?

  • A They have had little impact on the study of language.
  • B They have helped the study of linguistics to progress.
  • C They are not accepted by the majority of linguists.
  • D The assumption behind them is wrong.

Q31 In the final paragraph, the writer concludes that Alison Wray’s ideas will help establish a link between

  • A grammar and meaning.
  • B messages and proto-language.
  • C language, music and emotions.
  • D proto-language and modern semantics.
Questions 32–37
Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A-H, below.
The Société de Linguistique de Paris
Charles Darwin
John Blacking
Christiansen and Kirby
Derek Bickerton
Alison Wray
  • A suggested music was an essential part of every individual.
  • B made no link between music and language in a comprehensive study.
  • C believes that early language was very musical.
  • D felt that the origin of language should not be debated.
  • E states that early language was made up of basic words used in an unsystematic way.
  • F devoted 17 chapters of a book to music.
  • G believes that proto-language had no individual words.
  • H referred to music in part of a book about the development of human beings.

Q33 Charles Darwin

Q34 John Blacking

Q35 Christiansen and Kirby

Q36 Derek Bickerton

Q37 Alison Wray

Questions 38–40
Choose THREE letters, A-G.

Q38 According to the writer, which THREE of the following areas have not been studied enough in order to understand the origin of language?

  • A evidence from prehistoric times
  • B intelligence
  • C individual sounds
  • D music
  • E emotions
  • F human intellect
  • G children’s language

reference:
Q27

干扰 你可能想选A（涉及的学科太多），但原文只是客观列举了多个学科在参与讨论，并没有说学科“太多”是导致进展缓慢的原因 。

句子 Linguists, psychologists, anthropologists and archaeologists now frequently debate the origin of language and have published many articles and books on this topic. And yet, despite almost frenzied activity, limited progress has been made. (第1段)

解析 第一段提到，尽管现在的研究活动几乎到了狂热的程度，但取得的进展却十分有限，这种强烈的反差表明缺乏进展是让人意外的 。

Q28

解析 第二段指出的“问题”是，现有的理论假设大脑越大语言能力越强，但这与“化石证据（尼安德特人脑更大）”和“考古证据（尼安德特人没语言能力）”相互冲突打脸 。

干扰 不要选B（化石证据不足），原文明确给出了实实在在的化石证据，问题出在这些证据与现有的理论假设完全矛盾 。

句子 Many theories to date rely on an assumed association between brain size and language abilities, without acknowledging the problem this creates: fossil evidence indicates that the Neanderthals had larger brains than modern humans, Homo sapiens, but archaeological evidence indicates that the Neanderthals lacked a capacity for language. (第2段)

Q29

解析 作者认为现代的理论家（如写《语言进化》却没有提音乐的作者们）有一堂重要的课需要从卢梭那里学习，这意味着现代学者应该多关注卢梭将音乐与语言结合起来研究的方法 。

干扰 别选C，后来的《Language Evolution》这本书在17个章节里完全没有提到音乐，和卢梭的观点截然相反，绝对不是“继承/反映（mirrored）”了卢梭的思想 。

句子 In contrast, Morten Christiansen and Simon Kirby's book, Language Evolution (2000), which they conceived as 'a definitive book on the subject', failed to mention music in any of its 17 chapters. Those authors have an important lesson to learn from Rousseau and other writers of his time who addressed the origin of language. (第4段)

Q30

句子 But Bickerton's idea that the precursor of modern language consisted of words strung together with limited, if any, grammar is, I believe, fundamentally mistaken... This idea has dominated the field of language origins for the last two decades, and is one that I once found persuasive. But I now understand that it is not only flawed but has severely limited the progress that should have been made. (第7段)

解析 作者直言不讳地说，Derek Bickerton 关于早期语言（proto-language）缺乏语法的假设，从根本上就是错误的（fundamentally mistaken） 。

干扰 你可能看到原文说他的观点“主导了过去二十年”，就想当然以为这是被广泛接受的好事，但作者紧接着就说这个想法不仅有缺陷，还严重阻碍了研究进展 。

Q31

解析 作者在文章结尾明确总结，Alison Wray 的见解能让我们理解音乐和语言的起源，并将这两者都与人类祖先的情感（emotional lives）生活联系起来 。

干扰 选项B只是 Alison Wray 理论内部的一个运作机制（语言由信息包构成），而不是作者认为该理论最终能帮助建立的宏大“联系（link）” 。

句子 For Wray, proto-language was semantically complex and agrammatical. I believe this insight enables us to understand the origin of music as well as language, and to relate both to the emotional lives of our human ancestors. (第8段)

Q32

解析 1866年，巴黎语言学会直接“禁止（banned）”了所有关于语言起源的讨论，这完美对应选项D“认为不应该被讨论” 。

干扰 不要想得太复杂，这里的“banned all discussions”是非常直白的字面替换，没有任何深层引申意思 。

句子 However, the debate became plagued by strange theories, so much so that in 1866 the influential Société de Linguistique de Paris banned all discussions about the origin of language. (第1段)

Q33

解析 达尔文在他关于“人类进化（human evolution）”的书中，花了数页篇幅专门讨论音乐的发展，这对应选项H“在一本关于人类发展的书中提到了音乐” 。

干扰 选项F“花了17章写音乐”是张冠李戴，写了17章却只字没提音乐的是后来的 Christiansen and Kirby 。

句子 One is the aforementioned Charles Darwin who, in his 1871 book on human evolution, The Descent of Man, devoted several pages to the development of music. (第3段)

Q34

干扰 只要抓住“universal（普遍的）”和“every individual（每个个体）”这两个词的同义替换，这道题就能瞬间锁定 。

句子 Another is the renowned ethnomusicologist John Blacking, whose 1973 book, How Musical is Man?, broached the idea that music is an inherent and universal human quality. (第3段)

解析 John Blacking 提出，音乐是人类“与生俱来且普遍的特质（inherent and universal human quality）”，这直接对应选项A“音乐是每个个体的核心部分” 。

Q35

解析 Christiansen 和 Kirby 写了一本关于语言进化的“权威著作（definitive book）”，但在17个章节中却对音乐只字未提，这对应选项B“在全面研究中没有将音乐与语言建立联系” 。

干扰 你可能只看到了“17 chapters”就急着选F，但原文白纸黑字写的是“failed to mention music（没有提到音乐）”，一定要把句子看完 。

句子 In contrast, Morten Christiansen and Simon Kirby's book, Language Evolution (2000), which they conceived as 'a definitive book on the subject', failed to mention music in any of its 17 chapters. (第4段)

Q36

解析 Derek Bickerton 认为语言的前身是由缺乏语法的“词（words）”串在一起组成的，这对应选项E“早期语言由基本词汇组成，使用方式不系统（无语法）” 。

干扰 虽然他在讲早期语言，但他认为这种语言依然是由一个个“词（words）”构成的，千万不要和后来 Alison Wray 认为“没有单个词（no individual words）”的观点搞混淆了 。

句子 But Bickerton's idea that the precursor of modern language consisted of words strung together with limited, if any, grammar is, I believe, fundamentally mistaken. (第7段)

Q37

句子 By this she means that the precursor to language was a communication system composed of 'messages' rather than words... But in Wray's proto-language, they were not composed out of smaller units of meaning (i.e. words) which could be combined together using a rule system (i.e. grammar)... (第8段)

解析 Alison Wray 认为早期语言是由“信息（messages）”构成的整体，而“不是由更小的意义单位（即词汇）组合而成的”，这对应选项G“早期语言没有单个词汇” 。

干扰 这里的“not composed out of smaller units of meaning (i.e. words)”是解题的绝对核心，明确否定了单个词汇的存在 。

Q38

解析 作者列举的第一个研究不足的原因是，对我们人类祖先的“考古学和化石证据（archaeological and fossil proof）”关注不够，这精准对应选项A的史前时代证据 。

干扰 选项F“human intellect（人类智力）”是已经被广泛研究过的领域（put significant effort into examining the intellectual capacities），作者指出的是缺乏对智力背后的实物化石证据的关注 。

句子 I believe there are four reasons for this. The first is an insufficient concern with the archaeological and fossil proof of the brains and behaviour of our human ancestors. (第2段)

Q39

解析 作者列出的第二个导致进展有限的原因，是对现代人类另一个主要的交流系统——“音乐（music）”——的关注严重不足 。

干扰 文章明确列出了几条“insufficient concern with...”的内容，这里的定位非常直接，不需要去过度推敲其他干扰项 。

句子 That 'something' might relate to the second reason for limited progress: insufficient concern with the other major aural and vocal communication system of modern humans: music. (第3段)

Q40

解析 作者指出的第三个缺乏进展的原因是，对“情感（emotion）”的关注不够，研究者过于关注智力而忽视了祖先的情感生活 。

干扰 原文直接写了“an insufficient concern with emotion”，这道多选题其实就是送分题，只要顺着文章结构找到作者列出的几个原因就能一一对应拿分 。

句子 That question leads directly to a third reason for our lack of progress in understanding how language evolved, and indeed the human mind in general: an insufficient concern with emotion... their emotional lives have been sorely neglected. (第5段)
